sections.h2: Your options for a fast sale in Lower Makefield Township
sections.html:
You have three ways to go: hire an agent, sell on your own, or accept a cash offer. Cash is the quickest, since settlement happens when you are ready and not when a buyer's lender signs off. The township's own sale steps are light: a moving permit, a sewer lateral inspection by the seller, and clean tax and utility balances.

Houses on this side of the Delaware are expensive, and every idle month adds up through insurance, utilities and tax bills. Owners who want out fast rarely cite price alone. Common reasons are an estate to close out, a job move, a divorce, a rental that wore the landlord down, or repairs the owner would rather not pay for.

  • Cash purchase: the house goes as it stands and the date is yours to pick.
  • Agent listing: wider exposure and often a better price, in return for showings, repair requests and a slower pace.
  • For-sale-by-owner: the commission stays with you, and so do the marketing, the contract and the haggling.

Lower Makefield lies on the Delaware in Bucks County and surrounds the borough of Yardley, which is why most addresses carry a Yardley mailing label even though they are in Lower Makefield. Children attend the Pennsbury School District, and Interstate 295 is the main highway into New Jersey.

An estimated 34,028 people live here. Owners live in 87.6 percent of occupied homes. A typical owned home is valued at $630,200 and a typical rent is $2,340. Nearly every sale is a single-family house with an owner in residence. Prices at this level make every percentage point of transfer tax and every month of carrying cost visible, so compare closing timelines as carefully as the offer price.

Winter freezes are a fact of life here, so expect a buyer's inspector to focus on roof, gutters and basement. Having recent repair records on hand helps.

sections.h2: Property taxes on a Lower Makefield home
sections.html:
Real estate tax comes from three bills: township, county and the Pennsbury School District. The 2025 combined rate is 256.403 mills, and the township levies no earned income tax.

Combined 2025 tax rate, by taxing body
Taxing bodyMills
Lower Makefield Township24.95
Bucks County27.45
Pennsbury School District (2025-2026)204.003
Total256.403

A mill equals a tenth of a percent of assessed value. The township and county send their bills near March 1. Pay within two months and you get a 2 percent discount, pay within four months and you owe face amount, and after that a 10 percent penalty applies. The school bill arrives near July 1 and covers the school year. Once the collector's books close, delinquent accounts move to the Bucks County Tax Claim Bureau. At settlement these bills are prorated, and the tax office at 267-274-1116 can give you current figures.

sections.h2: What the township requires when you sell
sections.html:
Community development lists three sale items, and the township does not ask for a resale use and occupancy certificate. Phone 267-274-1100 to verify the list before you set a closing date, because a buyer's contract may add conditions of its own.

  • A moving permit, one for each side of the sale.
  • A sewer lateral inspection by the seller, to catch problems with the private line. Questions and submissions go to sewerlateral@lmt.org.
  • Calls to the taxing authorities and utility companies for any additional requirements they impose.

Allow time for a plumber to scope the line and for the township to review the report, since a failed line has to be fixed. If you are working to a tight closing date, book the plumber the same week you accept an offer.

The county closes the yearly appeal window in early August, and whatever the board decides applies to the tax year after. An interim appeal runs on the date printed on a recent assessment revision notice. The Board of Assessment Appeals sits on the first and third Tuesday of every month at the Doylestown courthouse, phone 215-348-6219.

Owners who live in the house can apply for the homestead and farmstead exclusion, which lowers the value used for school tax. Apply by March 1 for the tax year starting the next July 1. Investors should know about a 2026 Pennsylvania law: after buying a property, the owner sends contact details to the Board within 30 days, though owner-occupied homes are excused.

Pennsylvania takes 1 percent of the sale value in transfer tax. Locally, the township and the school district each take a further half percent, which brings the total to 2 percent. Your sales contract assigns the shares between buyer and seller, and because the state holds both parties jointly responsible, settle that point in writing before you sign.

Certain family transfers and property passed by will or intestacy are exempt. A title company can price the statement of value and the recording fees due at the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds. Mention any payoff, lien or tenant early so the figures come back right.

sections.h2: Before you accept a cash offer
sections.html:
Run a quick net sheet first. Start with the likely list price, then subtract agent commission, the transfer tax share you would owe, repairs a buyer would demand, and the taxes and insurance you would pay while the house waits on the market. Compare that total with the cash figure in hand.

Also look at your own calendar. If you need to relocate, close an estate or end a lease by a fixed date, certainty can be worth more than the last bit of price. Cash Home Buyers CA can give you a figure to put next to your other choices, and you decide whether the numbers work.

After you accept an offer, work through four items. Apply for each side's moving permit. Have a plumber scope the sewer lateral and send the findings to the township. Ask the tax office and each utility whether it has a requirement of its own. The title company then builds the settlement statement, prorates the tax bills and files the deed.

A cash sale shortens the list further. Without a lender there is no appraisal and no loan approval, which leaves the sewer lateral report and the permits as the items that set your date. Start them first. If the plumber finds a problem with the private line, the repair becomes the longest step, and you will want to know that before you promise a closing day.

faqs.q: Does Lower Makefield Township require a resale certificate?
faqs.a: No. Community development confirms a resale use and occupancy certificate is not required. It does require a moving permit for buyer and seller and a sewer lateral inspection by the seller, so call the township office to confirm.

faqs.q: How much is transfer tax in Lower Makefield?
faqs.a: The state takes 1 percent, and the township and school district each add one half percent. The 2 percent total is split between buyer and seller as the contract says.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for the sewer lateral inspection?
faqs.a: The seller. The township expects the seller to inspect the private sewer line and submit the result, and its review can take time, so schedule the plumber early in your sale.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to challenge a Bucks County assessment?
faqs.a: Annual appeals close in early August, and a decision affects the following tax year. An interim appeal depends on the date shown on an assessment revision notice.

faqs.q: Which school district serves Lower Makefield Township?
faqs.a: Pennsbury School District serves the township, and its 2025-2026 millage of 204.003 is the largest part of the combined 256.403 mills on a Lower Makefield tax bill.
